query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. decision.trend: Research has focused on improving the mechanical properties of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) by adjusting composition, processing routes, and microstructure. Earlier studies have shown that RHEAs can exhibit good yield strength, but often at the expense of room-temperature fracture toughness or high density. Recent efforts have explored the use of various processing techniques, such as mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering, and hot isostatic pressing, to enhance the mechanical properties of RHEAs. Additionally, the introduction of secondary phases, such as precipitates or reinforcement particles, has been investigated to improve the strength and ductility of RHEAs.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in improving the mechanical properties of RHEAs, the trade-off between yield strength, fracture toughness, and density remains a significant challenge. The development of RHEAs with reduced density without sacrificing their strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance is still an open question.
decision.why: Spark plasma sintering has been shown to be effective in enhancing the mechanical properties of RHEAs by refining the microstructure and introducing secondary phases. This processing route may offer a promising approach to reducing the density of RHEAs while maintaining their mechanical performance.
